messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Fisherman
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 65

**Case Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 58-year-old South Asian man, a widower of five years, who presents to the clinic at the urging of his eldest son. He is a fisherman by trade, having worked the coastal waters of his home state for over three decades. He sits very still in the chair, his hands resting on his knees, his gaze fixed on a point on the floor. He speaks in a low, measured tone, as if each word costs him a great effort.

The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago, during the monsoon season. Mr. A. was the captain of a small trawler, a job he had done since he was a teenager. One night, a sudden, violent storm overturned his boat. He remembers the sound most clearly—a deafening, metallic screech of wind against the hull, then the shock of cold, black water. He was trapped under the capsized vessel for nearly an hour, his lungs burning, his fingers scrabbling against the slick metal of the hull in the absolute dark. He remembers the exact moment he stopped fighting, the strange, quiet peace that settled over him as he began to drown. He was rescued by a passing cargo ship, pulled from the water just as his consciousness faded.

Now, Mr. A. cannot go near the sea. The mere sight of it from his son’s apartment window, where he now lives, sends a violent tremor through his body. He describes it as “the water remembering me.” The smell of brine, once the smell of his livelihood and his freedom, now triggers a visceral nausea. He has not set foot on a dock in over a year. His fishing nets, coiled and dry, sit untouched in a corner of the storage room. He cannot bear to look at them; they feel like a shroud.

His sleep is a battleground. Every night, he is back in the overturned boat. He wakes gasping for air, his chest tight, his hands clawing at the sheets. He has thrown the clock radio across the room twice, mistaking its red digital glow for a warning light on the boat’s console. His son, who sleeps in the next room, finds him pacing the hallway at 3 a.m., muttering prayers in his native tongue. Mr. A. now avoids the bathroom at night because the sound of the toilet flushing sounds too much like water rushing into the hull.

His world has shrunk to the size of his son’s living room. He avoids the kitchen when his daughter-in-law is washing dishes. He flinches when a child splashes in a puddle. He has stopped attending the local temple, no longer able to hear the conch shell blown during the morning prayers—the sound is too close to the ship’s foghorn that signaled the storm. He feels a constant, low-grade dread, a sense of being “not quite here,” as if a part of him is still trapped in that freezing, silent darkness. He believes, with a quiet certainty, that he should have died that night. He tells me he feels “unfinished,” a ghost in his own life.

The most painful part, he says, is not the fear, but the loss of his identity. He was a provider, a captain, a man of the sea. Now, he is a guest in his son’s home, a man who cannot work, who cannot even bear to look out the window. He feels a deep, corrosive shame. He has stopped calling his old fishing partners. He cannot bear their pity, or the way they might see him as a man who broke. He spends his days watching the television with the sound off, the flickering images a meaningless blur. He is waiting, he says, but he does not know for what. He is a man adrift, not on the sea, but in the quiet, dry land of his own life.
